claims.text: In adults 60+ without prior CVD, initiating low-dose aspirin increases net cardiovascular harm: excess major bleeding (GI and intracranial) per 1,000 treated over about 5 years equals or exceeds the MI and ischemic stroke events prevented, under equal or bleeding-weighted severity weights.

In adults 60+ without prior CVD, initiating low-dose aspirin yields a small net reduction in cardiovascular harm over about 5 years, with prevented MI and ischemic stroke outweighing bleeding under a severity-weighted composite.
Net benefit from initiating aspirin in adults 60+ occurs only in a high-baseline-risk, low-bleeding-risk subgroup; for the average person aged 60+ the net balance is neutral or negative.
Initiating low-dose aspirin in adults 60+ has no net effect on cardiovascular harm; benefits and bleeding harms offset to within a net difference of about zero per 1,000 treated.
The net-harm question has no single answer because the sign depends on the weighting of nonfatal events versus bleeds, so any verdict is an artifact of the weights chosen.

Across primary prevention trials, low-dose aspirin reduces major CV events (MI, ischemic stroke, CV death) by roughly 8-15% relatively, which is about 1-3 fewer events per 1,000 treated over 5 years in older adults.
In participants aged 70+ (ASPREE), aspirin did not significantly reduce the CV composite (HR about 0.95, CI including 1) over a median of about 4.7 years.
Aspirin has no effect on major CV events in primary prevention in adults 60+.

Low-dose aspirin increases major bleeding by roughly 30-50% relatively, about 2-5 additional major bleeds per 1,000 treated over 5 years in adults 60+, with the excess concentrated in GI bleeding and rising with age.
Aspirin significantly increases intracranial hemorrhage in adults 60+, by at least 0.5 per 1,000 over 5 years.
Low-dose aspirin does not increase major bleeding in adults 60+ beyond chance.
In older adults, aspirin increased all-cause mortality, driven by cancer deaths, in ASPREE (HR about 1.14 overall), with no benefit on disability-free survival.
Aspirin has no effect on all-cause mortality, cancer incidence or mortality, or disability-free survival in older adults; any observed differences are chance findings.
Aspirin reduces long-term cancer incidence or mortality (especially colorectal) in adults 60+, offsetting some net harm.
The net balance is more favorable at higher baseline CV risk, but absolute bleeding excess rises with age and prior bleeding risk, so no 60+ subgroup shows reliable net benefit.
Some subgroups (for example, high 10-year CV risk adults aged 60-69 with low bleeding risk, or people with diabetes) have a net benefit from aspirin.
There is no credible heterogeneity of net effect by risk, age, diabetes, statin use, or bleeding risk; subgroup interactions are null.
Under equal weighting of MI, ischemic stroke, and major bleeding, the net effect per 1,000 treated over about 5 years in adults 60+ is harm or zero, not benefit.
Under weighting by case fatality or disability burden, so that bleeds count less than MI or stroke, the net effect per 1,000 treated is a small benefit.
The net effect is zero under any plausible weighting.

USPSTF 2022 recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention in adults 60+ (Grade D), and ACC/AHA 2019 advises against routine use in those over 70 or at increased bleeding risk, citing a bleeding excess that outweighs benefit.
Guidelines (ESC and others) recommend routine aspirin initiation for primary prevention in adults 60+.
